blocks.en: Abstract
blocks.zh: 摘要

blocks.en: We identify a key limitation of existing feed-forward 3DGS methods: Gaussian attributes are typically predicted in a radial-distance-normalized space that canonicalizes a global radial statistic of the reconstructed geometry, while the spacing between neighboring Gaussian centers can still vary substantially across scene scales and camera configurations. This mismatch induces systematic shifts in Gaussian-scale targets, leading to ambiguous supervision. To address this, we propose SplatAnything with Gaussian Spacing Normalization (GSNorm), which canonicalizes a robust scene-level statistic of Gaussian spacing to provide a more consistent spatial reference for Gaussian prediction. To rigorously assess our method, we further establish a systematic benchmark spanning diverse datasets, input sparsity levels, and challenging extrapolated viewpoints. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SplatAnything achieves state-of-the-art performance, with particularly strong gains under substantial variations in scene scale and viewpoint.
blocks.zh: 我们发现,现有的向导3DGS方法有一个关键限制: 高斯的属性一般在一个光圈-距离-常态化的空间中进行预测,该空间能够对重建的几何学进行全局的光圈统计,而相邻的高斯中心之间的间隔仍然可以因场景尺度和相机配置而有很大差异. 这种不匹配导致高斯级目标发生系统性转变,导致监管模棱两可. 为了解决这个问题,我们提议用高斯中程常态化(GSNorm)来标注任何事物,它将高斯间距的强烈场景级统计可以用来为高斯的预测提供更一致的空间参考. 为了严格评估我们的方法,我们进一步确立了一个系统的基准,涵盖不同的数据集、输入伸缩度水平和具有挑战性的推论观点。 广泛的实验表明,Splating Anything实现了最先进的性能,在场景规模和视角的巨大差异下,特别显著的收获.

blocks.en: 1 Introduction
blocks.zh: 导言

blocks.en:
Feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) directly predicts a 3D
Gaussian representation ( Kerbl et al., 2023 ) from input images, avoiding
the costly per-scene optimization of conventional 3DGS.
This efficiency makes it attractive for large-scale 3D reconstruction and
digital content creation.
The ultimate goal is a single model that generalizes reliably across
arbitrary scene scales, camera configurations, and target viewpoints, yet
such broad generalization remains challenging.

geometry foundation model ( Wang et al., 2025 ; Lin et al., 2025 ; Team et al., 2026 ; Jiang et al., 2026 ; Yu et al., 2026 ) ,

blocks.en:
To address this issue, we introduce SplatAnything , a
feed-forward 3DGS framework equipped with Gaussian Spacing
Normalization (GSNorm) . The key idea of GSNorm is to derive the
scene-level normalization factor from a representative statistic of
Gaussian spacing, rather than from a global radial statistic. Under the
per-pixel Gaussian prediction paradigm, where each valid image pixel
corresponds to a Gaussian center, perspective projection relates Gaussian
spacing to scene depth and camera intrinsics. Based on this relation,
GSNorm computes Gaussian spacing over all valid observations and uses its
median as a robust scene-level normalization factor. The reconstructed
geometry is then rescaled accordingly, canonicalizing the representative
Gaussian spacing across scenes. This provides a more consistent spatial reference for Gaussian-scale prediction, alleviating ambiguity in supervision caused by variations in
scene scale and camera configuration and thereby improving generalization
across diverse scenes and viewpoints.

introduce a cross-dataset benchmark for in-the-wild evaluation.

blocks.en: 2 Related Work
blocks.zh: 2 相关工作

blocks.en:
Recent feed-forward geometry foundation models ( Wang et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2025 ; Lin et al., 2025 ; Liu et al., 2025 ; Jiang et al., 2026 ) directly recover depth, point maps, and camera poses from RGB observations, providing strong geometric priors across diverse scenes.
These models typically employ radial distance normalization to keep reconstructed geometry within a numerically stable range. While effective for geometry prediction, such normalization does not ensure consistent Gaussian spacing across scenes, cameras, and image resolutions. This becomes critical when the normalized geometry is reused for per-pixel Gaussian prediction, since Gaussian scales are defined in the same 3D coordinate system.
blocks.zh:
近代饲料向上几何地基模型(王等,2024;王等,2025;林等,2025;刘等,2025;蒋等,2026) 从RGB观测中直接取回深度,点地图,相机所浮出水面,提供了跨越多景的强几何前身.
这些模型通常采用射线相距正常化,使重建的几何学保持在数字稳定的范围内. 虽然对几何预测有效,但这种正常化并不能确保连续高斯相距跨越场景,相机和图像分辨率. 这在常态几何被再用到每像素高斯预测时变得至关重要,因为高斯平分被定义在同一3D坐标系统中.

blocks.en:
Feed-forward 3DGS methods directly infer Gaussian representations from image observations, often by first estimating per-pixel depth and then predicting Gaussian attributes. pixelSplat ( Charatan et al., 2024 ) reconstructs 3D Gaussians from image pairs by learning a 3D probability distribution over Gaussian centers. DepthSplat ( Xu et al., 2025b ) combines monocular depth priors with multi-view matching, while ReSplat ( Xu et al., 2025a ) further refines predicted Gaussians through rendering-based optimization. However, limited geometric accuracy can become a bottleneck under large viewpoint extrapolation.
More recent methods ( Jiang et al., 2025 ; Lin et al., 2025 ; Team et al., 2026 ; Anonymous, 2027 ) leverage strong geometry foundation models
to initialize Gaussian centers and predict the remaining attributes.
Although this substantially improves reconstruction quality, these
methods still inherit the radial-distance-normalized space of their
geometry backbones, in which Gaussian spacing can vary substantially
across scene scales and camera configurations, leading to ambiguity in
Gaussian-scale supervision. Such supervision ambiguity makes it difficult
to learn a single Gaussian predictor that generalizes reliably across
diverse input settings.
Other approaches ( An et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2026 ) do not rely on
explicit geometric priors. While they can achieve strong rendering
quality at interpolated viewpoints, the learned Gaussian geometry can
become less reliable under large viewpoint extrapolation.

Table 3 , comparing RDNorm,

For RDNorm with scale calibration, Gaussian prediction remains in the

blocks.en: 5 Conclusion
blocks.zh: 5 结论

blocks.en:
We identified a key limitation of existing methods: Radial Distance
Normalization (RDNorm) does not directly normalize Gaussian spacing,
leading to ambiguity in Gaussian-scale supervision across scene scales and
camera configurations. To address this issue, we introduced SplatAnything with Gaussian Spacing Normalization (GSNorm) ,
which derives a scene-level normalization factor from a representative
statistic of Gaussian spacing and provides a more consistent spatial
reference for Gaussian prediction. We further established a systematic
cross-dataset benchmark covering different input sparsity levels and
challenging extrapolated viewpoints. Experiments demonstrate that
SplatAnything achieves the strongest performance across most evaluation
settings, highlighting the effectiveness of GSNorm and marking a
substantial step toward feed-forward 3DGS.

blocks.en:
We construct source views to cover diverse camera-motion patterns while maintaining sufficient geometric overlap for reliable reconstruction by the geometry foundation model. We consider four representative trajectory
patterns: forward-traversal , where the camera moves primarily along the viewing direction; lateral-sweep , where the camera translates mainly sideways while maintaining a similar viewing direction; outward-looking , where the camera remains approximately stationary and rotates to observe different directions; and inward-orbit , where the camera moves around a local region while maintaining an inward-facing view toward that region. For trajectories with substantial translation, we further vary the sampling stride to produce either densely overlapping or wide-baseline source views, covering different levels of parallax and input sparsity. During training, the trajectory pattern and sampling stride are randomly selected from a dataset-specific mixture, with distance and stride budgets adapted to each dataset. Validation uses a fixed deterministic sampling configuration for reproducibility. Examples of the different source-view sampling patterns are shown in Fig. 8 .

designed to independently control input-view sparsity and target-view

blocks.en:
Instead of distributing the source views uniformly over the entire
capture, we sample them from a compact contiguous arc of the camera
trajectory. This design leaves a meaningful portion of the capture
outside the observed region, making it possible to evaluate genuinely
extrapolated novel views rather than views that are always bracketed by
the inputs.
To make different input-view counts directly comparable, we adopt a fixed-span strategy. For each scene, we first determine the
trajectory span at the sparsest setting of 4 4 source views. We select
the widest arc whose adjacent source-view pairs maintain sufficient
geometric overlap, measured by symmetric co-visibility; specifically,
the 20 20 -th percentile of adjacent-pair co-visibility is required to be
at least 0.35 0.35 . The resulting span and offset are then reused for 8 8 , 16 16 , 32 32 , and 64 64 views, with additional views inserted within
the same trajectory range. Therefore, all view-count settings share the
same spatial coverage, and only the observation density changes. This
allows the effect of input sparsity to be evaluated without conflating
it with changes in scene coverage.

For each candidate target view, valid pixels are back-projected using

geometrically consistent with at least one source view are treated as
observed, while occluded and out-of-frustum pixels reduce the overlap
score; pixels for which visibility cannot be determined due to invalid
depth are excluded from the statistic.

remain high even under a substantial viewpoint change. We evaluate up
to 40 40 candidate target views per scene and retain those whose symmetric

During training, the predicted Gaussians are rendered using the
ground-truth target camera poses for supervision. However, the camera
trajectory and depth predicted by the geometry model generally have an
arbitrary global scale relative to the ground-truth trajectory. Directly
combining the predicted depth with the ground-truth poses would therefore
lead to inconsistent geometry and camera scales, resulting in misaligned
rendering supervision.
To resolve this scale ambiguity, we estimate a scene-level alignment factor
from the predicted and ground-truth source-camera trajectories. Specifically,
we compute the ratio between corresponding pairwise camera baselines and use
their median as a robust global scale factor. The predicted depth maps are
then rescaled by this factor and back-projected using the ground-truth
source-camera poses to construct Gaussian centers in the ground-truth
coordinate system. The resulting Gaussians can therefore be rendered
directly using the ground-truth target-camera poses for supervision. This
alignment is applied to both the pose-free and pose-conditioned variants,
since the predicted camera trajectory can exhibit a global scale discrepancy
with respect to the ground truth in either setting.

blocks.en:
GSNorm canonicalizes the representative single-view point spacing across scenes and camera configurations, but it does not by itself eliminate the variation in primitive density caused by multi-view accumulation. Since each valid pixel predicts a Gaussian primitive, increasing the number of input views over the same spatial region can introduce multiple Gaussians at nearby 3D locations, making the resulting primitive density dependent on the number of overlapping observations. To reduce such redundancy, we apply a spatial voxel merging strategy following AnySplat ( Jiang et al., 2025 ) . Specifically, we predict a per-pixel weight map w p = { w i p } i = 1 N w^{p}=\{w_{i}^{p}\}_{i=1}^{N} and merge redundant per-view Gaussians within local voxels. This produces the final unified 3D Gaussian scene representation 𝒢 \mathcal{G} .
GSNorm and voxel merging therefore address two complementary sources of scale variation: GSNorm provides a consistent characteristic sampling scale for Gaussian prediction across scenes, whereas voxel merging regularizes the accumulation of primitives caused by overlapping multi-view observations. Together, they allow the model to operate robustly over varying numbers of input views.
